**Martin Van Buren**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-5) (December 5, 1782–July 24, 1862) was the eighth [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), serving from 1837 to 1841. Van Buren co-founded the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") with [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") and became Jackson's [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") from 1833 to 1837.

Van Buren was born in [Kinderhook, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinderhook,_New_York "Kinderhook, New York"), where most residents were of [Dutch descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Americans "Dutch Americans") and spoke [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language") as their primary language. He is the only president to have spoken English as a second language. Van Buren entered politics as a member of the [Democratic-Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party"), won a seat in the [New York State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Senate "New York State Senate") in 1813, and was elected to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") in 1821. As the leader of the [Bucktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucktails "Bucktails") faction of the party, he established the political machine known as the [Albany Regency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_Regency "Albany Regency"). Van Buren ran successfully for governor of New York to support Andrew Jackson's candidacy in the [1828 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1828_United_States_presidential_election "1828 United States presidential election") but resigned shortly after Jackson was inaugurated so he could accept appointment as Jackson's secretary of state. In the cabinet, Van Buren was a key Jackson advisor and built the organizational structure for the coalescing Democratic Party. He ultimately resigned to help resolve the [Petticoat affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petticoat_affair "Petticoat affair") and briefly served as ambassador to the United Kingdom. At Jackson's behest, the [1832 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1832_Democratic_National_Convention "1832 Democratic National Convention") nominated Van Buren for vice president, and he took office after the Democratic ticket won the 1832 presidential election.

With Jackson's strong support and the organizational strength of the Democratic Party, Van Buren successfully ran for president in the 1836 presidential election. However, his popularity soon eroded because of his response to the [Panic of 1837](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1837 "Panic of 1837"), which centered on his [Independent Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Treasury "Independent Treasury") system, a plan under which the federal government of the United States would store its funds in vaults rather than in banks. More conservative Democrats and Whigs in Congress ultimately delayed Van Buren's plan from being implemented until 1840. [His presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren "Presidency of Martin Van Buren") was further marred by the costly [Second Seminole War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Seminole_War "Second Seminole War") and his refusal to admit [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Texas "Republic of Texas") to the [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") as a [slave state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_states_and_free_states "Slave states and free states"). In 1840, he lost his [re-election bid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1840_United_States_presidential_election "1840 United States presidential election") to [William Henry Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Harrison "William Henry Harrison"). While Van Buren is praised for anti-slavery stances, in historical rankings, historians and political scientists often [rank him as a below-average U.S. president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "Historical rankings of presidents of the United States"), due to his handling of the Panic of 1837.

He was initially the leading candidate for the Democratic Party's nomination again in 1844, but his continued opposition to the [annexation of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_annexation "Texas annexation") angered Southern Democrats, leading to the nomination of [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk"). Van Buren grew increasingly opposed to slavery, and was the presidential nominee of the newly formed [Free Soil Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Soil_Party "Free Soil Party") in the [1848 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1848_United_States_presidential_election "1848 United States presidential election"), and his candidacy helped [Whig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)") nominee [Zachary Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor "Zachary Taylor") defeat Democrat [Lewis Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Cass "Lewis Cass"). Worried about sectional tensions, Van Buren returned to the Democratic Party after 1848 but was disappointed with the pro-southern presidencies of [Franklin Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce "Franklin Pierce") and [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan").

During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), Van Buren was a [War Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Democrat "War Democrat") who supported the policies of President [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln"), a [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"). Van Buren died of [asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma") at his home in Kinderhook in 1862, aged 79.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Further information: [Family of Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_of_Martin_Van_Buren "Family of Martin Van Buren")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/%22The_Birthplace_of_President_Martin_Van_Buren_in_Kinderhook%2C_New_York%22%2C_by_J.W._Barber.jpg/250px-%22The_Birthplace_of_President_Martin_Van_Buren_in_Kinderhook%2C_New_York%22%2C_by_J.W._Barber.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%22The_Birthplace_of_President_Martin_Van_Buren_in_Kinderhook,_New_York%22,_by_J.W._Barber.jpg)

Van Buren's birthplace by [John Warner Barber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Warner_Barber "John Warner Barber")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Martin_Van_Buren_Baptism_record.jpg/250px-Martin_Van_Buren_Baptism_record.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin_Van_Buren_Baptism_record.jpg)

Baptismal record with the Dutch spelling of Van Buren's first name, "Maarten"

Martin Van Buren was born on December 5, 1782, in [Kinderhook, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinderhook,_New_York "Kinderhook, New York"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-6) His father, [Abraham Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Van_Buren "Abraham Van Buren"), was a descendant of Cornelis Maessen, a native of [Buurmalsen, Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buurmalsen "Buurmalsen"), who had emigrated to [New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland "New Netherland") in 1631 and purchased a plot of land on [Manhattan Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Island "Manhattan Island").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole19843,_9-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWidmer2005153%E2%80%93165-8) Van Buren was the first president born after the Declaration of Independence and the last born prior to British ratification of the terms of the 1783 [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1783) "Treaty of Paris (1783)") that ended the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). As a result, he was the last president to be born, (but not last to serve) a 'jus soli' [British Subject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Subject "British Subject") by birth in one of the Thirteen Colonies. Abraham Van Buren had been a [patriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution) "Patriot (American Revolution)") during the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-10) and he later joined the [Democratic-Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-11) Abraham owned an inn and tavern in Kinderhook and served as Kinderhook's town clerk for several years. In 1776, he married Maria Hoes (or Goes) Van Alen (1746–1818) in the town of Kinderhook, also of Dutch extraction and the widow of Johannes Van Alen (1744–c.1773). She had three children from her first marriage, including future U.S. Representative [James I. Van Alen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_I._Van_Alen "James I. Van Alen"). Her second marriage produced five children, of which Martin was the third.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven19835%E2%80%936-12)

Van Buren received a basic education at the village schoolhouse, and briefly studied [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") at the [Kinderhook Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinderhook_Academy "Kinderhook Academy") and at [Washington Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claverack_College "Claverack College") in [Claverack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claverack,_New_York "Claverack, New York").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole198414-14) He had entirely Dutch ancestry and was raised speaking primarily Dutch, but he learned English while attending school[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-15) and is the only president of the United States whose first language was not English.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWidmer20056%E2%80%937-16) Also during his childhood, Van Buren learned at his father's inn how to interact with people from varied ethnic, income, and societal groups, which he used to his advantage as a political organizer.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-17) Van Buren's formal education ended in 1796, when he began [reading law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_law "Reading law") at the office of [Peter Silvester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Silvester_(1734%E2%80%931808) "Peter Silvester (1734–1808)") and his son Francis.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrooke2010230-18)

Van Buren, at 5 feet 6 inches (1.68 m) tall, was small in stature, and affectionately nicknamed "Little Van".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-19) He was also called the "Red Fox" due to his "bushy reddish sideburns, striking forehead and prominent nose".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-20) When Van Buren began his legal studies he wore rough, homespun clothing,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-21) causing the Silvesters to admonish him to pay greater heed to his clothing and personal appearance as an aspiring lawyer. He accepted their advice, and subsequently emulated the Silvesters' clothing, appearance, bearing, and conduct.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-22)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-23) The lessons Van Buren learned from the Silvesters were reflected in his career as a lawyer and politician, in which Van Buren was known for his amiability and fastidious appearance.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-24) Despite Kinderhook's strong affiliation with the [Federalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalist_Party "Federalist Party"), of which the Silvesters were also strong supporters, Van Buren adopted his father's Democratic-Republican leanings.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven19838%E2%80%939-25) The Silvesters and Democratic-Republican political figure [John Peter Van Ness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peter_Van_Ness "John Peter Van Ness") suggested that Van Buren's political leanings constrained him to complete his education with a Democratic-Republican attorney, so Van Buren spent a final year of apprenticeship in the New York City office of John Van Ness's brother [William P. Van Ness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_P._Van_Ness "William P. Van Ness"), a political lieutenant of [Aaron Burr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Burr "Aaron Burr").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198310%E2%80%9311-26) Van Ness introduced Van Buren to the intricacies of New York state politics, and Van Buren observed Burr's battles for control of the state Democratic-Republican party against [George Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Clinton_(vice_president) "George Clinton (vice president)") and [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston_(chancellor) "Robert R. Livingston (chancellor)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198314%E2%80%9315-27) He returned to Kinderhook in 1803, after his [admission to the New York bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admission_to_the_bar_in_the_United_States "Admission to the bar in the United States").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198315%E2%80%9317-28)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Hannah_van_buren_2.jpg/250px-Hannah_van_buren_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hannah_van_buren_2.jpg)

[Hannah Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Van_Buren "Hannah Van Buren")

Van Buren married [Hannah Hoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Van_Buren "Hannah Van Buren") in [Catskill, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catskill,_New_York "Catskill, New York"), on February 21, 1807, when he was 24 years old and she was 23. She was his childhood sweetheart and a daughter of his maternal first cousin, Johannes Dircksen Hoes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-29) She grew up in [Valatie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valatie,_New_York "Valatie, New York"), and like Van Buren, her home life was primarily Dutch as she spoke Dutch as her first language, and spoke English with a marked accent.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-30) The couple had six children, four of whom lived to adulthood: [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Van_Buren_II "Abraham Van Buren II") (1807–1873), unnamed daughter (stillborn around 1809), [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Van_Buren "John Van Buren") (1810–1866), Martin Jr. (1812–1855), Winfield Scott (born and died in 1814), and Smith Thompson (1817–1876).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MVLiB-31) Hannah contracted [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis"), and died in Kinderhook on February 5, 1819.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilbey200227-32) Martin Van Buren never remarried.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-33)

## Early political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early political career")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Martin_Van_Buren_1.png/250px-Martin_Van_Buren_1.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin_Van_Buren_1.png)

Painting of Van Buren by Daniel Dickinson, 1844

Upon returning to Kinderhook in 1803, Van Buren formed a law partnership with his half-brother, James Van Alen, and became financially secure enough to increase his focus on politics.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-34) Van Buren had been active in politics from age 18, if not before. In 1801, he attended a [Democratic-Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party") convention in [Troy, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy,_New_York "Troy, New York"), where he worked successfully to secure for John Peter Van Ness the party nomination in a special election for the [6th Congressional District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York's_6th_congressional_district "New York's 6th congressional district") seat.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrooke2010283-35) Upon returning to Kinderhook, Van Buren broke with the Burr faction, becoming an ally of both [DeWitt Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeWitt_Clinton "DeWitt Clinton") and [Daniel D. Tompkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_D._Tompkins "Daniel D. Tompkins"). After the faction led by Clinton and Tompkins dominated the 1807 elections, Van Buren was appointed [Surrogate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probate_court "Probate court") of [Columbia County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_County,_New_York "Columbia County, New York").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198318%E2%80%9322-36) Seeking a better base for his political and legal career, Van Buren and his family moved to the town of [Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson,_New_York "Hudson, New York"), the seat of Columbia County, in 1808.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198323%E2%80%9324-37) Van Buren's legal practice continued to flourish, and he traveled all over the state to represent various clients.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198325%E2%80%9326-38)

In 1812, Van Buren won his party's nomination for a seat in the [New York State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Senate "New York State Senate"). Though several Democratic-Republicans, including John Peter Van Ness, joined with the Federalists to oppose his candidacy, Van Buren won election to the state senate in mid-1812.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198329%E2%80%9332-39) Later in the year, the United States entered the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") against Great Britain, while Clinton launched an unsuccessful bid to defeat President [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison") in the [1812 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1812_United_States_presidential_election "1812 United States presidential election"). After the election, Van Buren became suspicious that Clinton was working with the Federalist Party, and he broke from his former political ally.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198333%E2%80%9339-40)

During the War of 1812, Van Buren worked with Clinton, Governor Tompkins, and [Ambrose Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrose_Spencer "Ambrose Spencer") to support the Madison administration's prosecution of the war.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198341%E2%80%9342-41) In addition, he was a special judge advocate appointed to serve as a prosecutor of [William Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hull "William Hull") during Hull's court-martial following the [surrender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Detroit "Siege of Detroit") of Detroit.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-42)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-43) Anticipating another military campaign, he collaborated with [Winfield Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott") on ways to reorganize the New York Militia in the winter of 1814–1815, but the end of the war halted their work in early 1815.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-44) Van Buren was so favorably impressed by Scott that he named his fourth son after him.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198343-45) Van Buren's strong support for the war boosted his standing, and in 1815, he was elected [New York Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Attorney_General "New York Attorney General"). Van Buren moved from Hudson to the state capital of [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York"), where he established a legal partnership with [Benjamin Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin_Butler_(lawyer) "Benjamin Franklin Butler (lawyer)"),[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198348%E2%80%9350-46) and shared a house with political ally [Roger Skinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Skinner "Roger Skinner").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-47) In 1816, Van Buren won re-election to the state senate, and he continued to simultaneously serve as attorney general.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198351%E2%80%9352-48) In 1819, he played an active part in prosecuting the accused murderers of Richard Jennings, the first murder-for-hire case in the state of New York.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-49)

### Albany Regency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Albany Regency")]

After Tompkins was elected as vice president in the [1816 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1816_United_States_presidential_election "1816 United States presidential election"), Clinton defeated Van Buren's preferred candidate, [Peter Buell Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Buell_Porter "Peter Buell Porter"), in the [1817 New York gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1817_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1817 New York gubernatorial election").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198358%E2%80%9359-50) Clinton threw his influence behind the construction of the [Erie Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_Canal "Erie Canal"), an ambitious project designed to connect [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie") to the Atlantic Ocean.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198361%E2%80%9362-51) Though many of Van Buren's allies urged him to block Clinton's canal bill, Van Buren believed the canal would benefit the state. His support for the bill helped it win approval from the New York legislature.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198363%E2%80%9364-52) Despite his support for the Erie Canal, Van Buren became the leader of an anti-Clintonian faction in New York known as the "[Bucktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucktails "Bucktails")".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198362-53)

The Bucktails succeeded in emphasizing party loyalty. Through his use of patronage, loyal newspapers, and connections with local party officials and leaders, Van Buren established what became known as the "[Albany Regency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_Regency "Albany Regency")", a [political machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_machine "Political machine") that emerged as an important factor in New York politics.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198364%E2%80%9365-54) The Regency relied on a coalition of small farmers, but also enjoyed support from the [Tammany Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammany_Hall "Tammany Hall") machine in New York City.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983110-55) During this era, Van Buren largely determined Tammany Hall's political policy for New York's Democratic-Republicans.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazo30-56)

A New York state referendum that expanded state voting rights to all white men in 1821, and which further increased the power of Tammany Hall, was guided by Van Buren.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-57) Although Governor Clinton remained in office until late 1822, Van Buren emerged as the leader of the state's Democratic-Republicans after the 1820 elections.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198381%E2%80%9382-58) Van Buren was a member of the 1820 state [constitutional convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_convention_(political_meeting) "Constitutional convention (political meeting)"), where he favored expanded voting rights, but opposed universal suffrage and tried to maintain property requirements for voting.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-59)

### Entry into national politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Entry into national politics")]

In February 1821, the state legislature [elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1821_United_States_Senate_election_in_New_York "1821 United States Senate election in New York") Van Buren to represent New York in the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven198392%E2%80%9393-60) Van Buren arrived in Washington during the "[Era of Good Feelings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Era_of_Good_Feelings "Era of Good Feelings")", a period in which partisan distinctions at the national level had faded.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198426%E2%80%9327-61) Van Buren quickly became a prominent figure in Washington, D.C., befriending [Secretary of the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Treasury "United States Secretary of the Treasury")[William H. Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Crawford "William H. Crawford"), among others.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983117-62) Though not an exceptional [orator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orator "Orator"), Van Buren frequently spoke on the [Senate floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_chamber "United States Senate chamber"), usually after extensively researching the subject at hand. Despite his commitments as a father and state party leader, Van Buren remained closely engaged in his legislative duties, and during his time in the Senate he was a member of the [Senate Finance Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance") and served as the chairman of the [Senate Judiciary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary "United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983176-64) As he gained renown, Van Buren earned monikers like "Little Magician" and "Sly Fox".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole1984432-65)

Van Buren chose to back Crawford over [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams"), [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), and [Henry Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay "Henry Clay") in the [presidential election of 1824](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1824_United_States_presidential_election "1824 United States presidential election").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983126%E2%80%93127-66) Crawford shared Van Buren's affinity for [Jeffersonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffersonian_democracy "Jeffersonian democracy") principles of [states' rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States'_rights "States' rights") and limited government, and Van Buren believed that Crawford was the ideal figure to lead a coalition of New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia's "[Richmond Junto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Junto "Richmond Junto")".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983129%E2%80%93130-67) Van Buren's support for Crawford aroused strong opposition in New York in the form of the People's party, which drew support from Clintonians, Federalists, and others opposed to Van Buren.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983139%E2%80%93140-68) Nonetheless, Van Buren helped Crawford win the Democratic-Republican party's presidential nomination at the February 1824 [congressional nominating caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_nominating_caucus "Congressional nominating caucus").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983143%E2%80%93144-69) The other Democratic-Republican candidates in the race refused to accept the poorly attended caucus's decision, and as the Federalist Party had all but ceased to function as a national party, the 1824 campaign became a competition among four candidates of the same party. Though Crawford suffered a severe stroke that left him in poor health, Van Buren continued to support his chosen candidate.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983145%E2%80%93146-70) In May 1824, Van Buren met with 81-year-old former President Thomas Jefferson in an attempt to bolster Crawford's candidacy, and though he was unsuccessful in gaining a public endorsement for Crawford, he nonetheless cherished the chance to meet with his political hero.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983146%E2%80%93148-71)

The 1824 elections dealt a severe blow to the Albany Regency, as Clinton returned to the governorship with the support of the People's party. By the time the state legislature convened to choose the state's [presidential electors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)"), results from other states had made it clear that no individual would win a majority of the electoral vote, necessitating a [contingent election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingent_election "Contingent election") in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983151%E2%80%93152-72) While Adams and Jackson finished in the top three and were eligible for selection in the contingent election, New York's electors would help determine whether Clay or Crawford would finish third.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983152%E2%80%93153-73) Though most of the state's electoral votes went to Adams, Crawford won one more electoral vote than Clay in the state, and Clay's defeat in Louisiana left Crawford in third place.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983156%E2%80%93157-74) With Crawford still in the running, Van Buren lobbied members of the House to support him.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983157%E2%80%93158-75) He hoped to engineer a Crawford victory on the second ballot of the contingent election, but Adams won on the first ballot with the help of Clay and [Stephen Van Rensselaer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Van_Rensselaer "Stephen Van Rensselaer"), a Congressman from New York. Despite his close ties with Van Buren, Van Rensselaer cast his vote for Adams, thus giving Adams a narrow majority of New York's delegation and a victory in the contingent election.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983158,_160%E2%80%93161-76)

After the House contest, Van Buren shrewdly kept out of the controversy which followed, and began looking forward to 1828. Jackson was angered to see the presidency go to Adams despite Jackson having won more popular votes than Adams had, and he eagerly looked forward to a rematch.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilbey200244-77) Jackson's supporters accused Adams and Clay of having made a "[corrupt bargain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrupt_bargain "Corrupt bargain")" in which Clay helped Adams win the contingent election in return for Clay's appointment as [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983164%E2%80%93165-78) Van Buren was always courteous in his treatment of opponents and showed no bitterness toward either Adams or Clay, and he voted to confirm Clay's nomination to the cabinet.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-79) At the same time, Van Buren opposed the Adams-Clay plans for [internal improvements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_improvements "Internal improvements") like roads and canals and declined to support U.S. participation in the [Congress of Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Panama "Congress of Panama").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole1984111-80) Van Buren considered Adams's proposals to represent a return to the [Hamiltonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton") economic model favored by Federalists, which he strongly opposed.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983163%E2%80%93164-81) Despite his opposition to Adams's public policies, Van Buren easily secured re-election in his divided home state in 1827.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983177%E2%80%93178-82)

### 1828 elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1828 elections")]

Van Buren's overarching goal at the national level was to restore a two-party system with party cleavages based on philosophical differences, and he viewed the old divide between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans as beneficial to the nation.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198427%E2%80%9328-83) Van Buren believed that these national parties helped ensure that elections were decided on national, rather than sectional or local, issues; as he put it, "party attachment in former times furnished a complete antidote for sectional prejudices". After the 1824 election, Van Buren was initially somewhat skeptical of Jackson, who had not taken strong positions on most policy issues. Nonetheless, he settled on Jackson as the one candidate who could beat Adams in the [1828 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1828_United_States_presidential_election "1828 United States presidential election"), and he worked to bring Crawford's former backers into line behind Jackson.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

He also forged alliances with other members of Congress opposed to Adams, including Vice President [John C. Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Calhoun "John C. Calhoun"), Senator [Thomas Hart Benton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hart_Benton_(politician) "Thomas Hart Benton (politician)"), and Senator [John Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Randolph_of_Roanoke "John Randolph of Roanoke").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983178%E2%80%93181-84) Seeking to solidify his standing in New York and bolster Jackson's campaign, Van Buren helped arrange the passage of the [Tariff of 1828](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff_of_Abominations "Tariff of Abominations"), which opponents labeled as the "Tariff of Abominations". The tariff was intended to protect northern and western agricultural products from foreign competition, but the resulting tax on imports cut into the profits of New England businessmen, who imported raw materials including iron to make into finished goods for subsequent resale, as well as finished goods including clothing for distribution and resale throughout the United States. The tariff also raised the cost of living in the South, because Southern states had little manufacturing capacity, which required them to export raw materials including cotton or sell them to Northern manufacturers, then import higher-priced finished goods or purchase them from the North. The tariff thus satisfied many who sought [protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectionism "Protectionism") from foreign competition, but angered Southern cotton interests and New England importers and manufacturers.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983196%E2%80%93199-85) Because Van Buren believed the South would never support Adams, and New England would never support Jackson, he was willing to alienate both regions through passage of the tariff.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983201-86)

Meanwhile, Clinton's death from a heart attack in 1828 dramatically shook up the politics of Van Buren's home state, while the [Anti-Masonic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Masonic_Party "Anti-Masonic Party") emerged as an increasingly important factor.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983194%E2%80%93196-87) After some initial reluctance, Van Buren chose to run for Governor of New York in the [1828 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_gubernatorial_election,_1828 "New York gubernatorial election, 1828").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983202%E2%80%93203,_209-88) Hoping that a Jackson victory would lead to his elevation to Secretary of State or Secretary of the Treasury, Van Buren chose [Enos T. Throop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enos_T._Throop "Enos T. Throop") as his running mate and preferred successor.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983209-89) Van Buren's candidacy was aided by the split between supporters of Adams, who had adopted the label of [National Republicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Republicans "National Republicans"), and the Anti-Masonic Party.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983206%E2%80%93208-90)

Reflecting his public association with Jackson, Van Buren accepted the gubernatorial nomination on a ticket that called itself "Jacksonian-Democrat".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983211-91) He campaigned on local as well as national issues, emphasizing his opposition to the policies of the Adams administration.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983211%E2%80%93212-92) Van Buren ran ahead of Jackson, winning the state by 30,000 votes compared to a margin of 5,000 for Jackson.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983214%E2%80%93215-93) Nationally, Jackson defeated Adams by a wide margin, winning nearly every state outside of New England.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson19849-94) After the election, Van Buren resigned from the Senate to start his term as governor, which began on January 1, 1829.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-95) While his term as governor was short, he did manage to pass the Bank Safety Fund Law, an early form of deposit insurance, through the legislature.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-96) He also appointed several key supporters, including [William L. Marcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_L._Marcy "William L. Marcy") and [Silas Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silas_Wright "Silas Wright"), to important state positions.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983218%E2%80%93219-97)

## Jackson administration (1829–1837)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Jackson administration (1829–1837)")]

### Secretary of State

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Secretary of State")]

Further information: [Petticoat affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petticoat_affair "Petticoat affair") and [Presidency of Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Andrew_Jackson "Presidency of Andrew Jackson")

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/62/Floride_Calhoun_nee_Colhoun.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Floride_Calhoun_nee_Colhoun.jpg)

Mrs. [Floride Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floride_Calhoun "Floride Calhoun"), a leader of the "petticoats"

In February 1829, Jackson wrote to Van Buren to ask him to become Secretary of State.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983228-98) Van Buren quickly agreed, and he resigned as governor the following month; his tenure of forty-three days is the shortest of any Governor of New York.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983229%E2%80%93231-99) No serious diplomatic crises arose during Van Buren's tenure as Secretary of State, but he achieved various successes, such as settling long-standing claims against France and winning reparations for property that had been seized during the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars"). He reached an agreement with the British to open trade with the [British West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_West_Indies "British West Indies") colonies and concluded a treaty with the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") that gained American merchants access to the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"). Items on which he did not achieve success included settling the [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine")-[New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick "New Brunswick") boundary dispute with Great Britain, gaining settlement of the U.S. claim to the [Oregon Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Country "Oregon Country"), concluding a commercial treaty with Russia, and persuading Mexico to sell [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole1984203-100)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MVB-101)

In addition to his foreign policy duties, Van Buren quickly emerged as an important advisor to Jackson on major domestic issues like the tariff and internal improvements.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983250%E2%80%93252-102) The Secretary of State was instrumental in convincing Jackson to issue the [Maysville Road veto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maysville_Road_veto "Maysville Road veto"), which both reaffirmed limited government principles and also helped prevent the construction of infrastructure projects that could potentially compete with New York's Erie Canal.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983261%E2%80%93262-103) He also became involved in a power struggle with Calhoun over appointments and other issues, including the [Petticoat Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petticoat_Affair "Petticoat Affair").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983245%E2%80%93247-104) The Petticoat Affair arose because [Peggy Eaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Eaton "Peggy Eaton"), wife of [Secretary of War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_War "United States Secretary of War")[John H. Eaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_H._Eaton "John H. Eaton"), was ostracized by the other cabinet wives due to the circumstances of her marriage.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-105)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-106)

Led by [Floride Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floride_Calhoun "Floride Calhoun"), wife of Vice President John Calhoun, the other cabinet wives refused to pay courtesy calls to the Eatons, receive them as visitors, or invite them to social events.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManweller2012[httpsbooksgooglecombooksiduqB3ehA7M0oCpgPA232_232]-107) As a widower, Van Buren was unaffected by the position of the cabinet wives.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-108) Van Buren initially sought to mend the divide in the cabinet, but most of the leading citizens in Washington continued to snub the Eatons.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983249%E2%80%93253-109) Jackson was close to Eaton, and he came to the conclusion that the allegations against Eaton arose from a plot against his administration led by Henry Clay.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983249,_253-110) The Petticoat Affair, combined with a contentious debate over the tariff and Calhoun's decade-old criticisms of Jackson's actions in the [First Seminole War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Seminole_War "First Seminole War"), contributed to a split between Jackson and Calhoun.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson19849%E2%80%9310-111) As the debate over the tariff and the proposed ability of South Carolina to [nullify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullification_(U.S._Constitution) "Nullification (U.S. Constitution)") federal law consumed Washington, Van Buren, not Calhoun, increasingly emerged as Jackson's likely successor.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983266-112)

The Petticoat affair was finally resolved when Van Buren offered to resign. In April 1831, Jackson accepted and reorganized his cabinet by asking for the resignations of the anti-Eaton cabinet members.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-113) Postmaster General [William T. Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_T._Barry "William T. Barry"), who had sided with the Eatons in the Petticoat Affair, was the lone cabinet member to remain in office.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-114) The cabinet reorganization removed Calhoun's allies from the Jackson administration, and Van Buren had a major role in shaping the new cabinet.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983266,_269%E2%80%93270-115) After leaving office, Van Buren continued to play a part in the [Kitchen Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitchen_Cabinet "Kitchen Cabinet"), Jackson's informal circle of advisors.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManweller2012[httpsbooksgooglecombooksiduqB3ehA7M0oCpgPA246_246]-116)

### Ambassador to Britain and vice presidency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Ambassador to Britain and vice presidency")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Francis_Alexander_-_Martin_Van_Buren_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Francis_Alexander_-_Martin_Van_Buren_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francis_Alexander_-_Martin_Van_Buren_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

A painting of Van Buren by [Francis Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Alexander_(painter) "Francis Alexander (painter)"), c.1830

In August 1831, Jackson gave Van Buren a [recess appointment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recess_appointment "Recess appointment") as the [ambassador to Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom "United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom"), and Van Buren arrived in London in September.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShepard1899224,_248-117) He was cordially received, but in February 1832, shortly after his 49th birthday, he learned that the Senate had rejected his nomination.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-118) The rejection of Van Buren was essentially the work of Calhoun.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole1984124-119) When the vote on Van Buren's nomination was taken, enough pro-Calhoun Jacksonians refrained from voting to produce a tie, which allowed Calhoun to cast the deciding vote against Van Buren.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-120)

Calhoun was elated, convinced that he had ended Van Buren's career. "It will kill him dead, sir, kill him dead. He will never kick, sir, never kick", Calhoun exclaimed to a friend.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2007378-121) Calhoun's move backfired; by making Van Buren appear the victim of petty politics, Calhoun raised Van Buren in both Jackson's regard and the esteem of others in the Democratic Party. Far from ending Van Buren's career, Calhoun's action gave greater impetus to Van Buren's candidacy for vice president.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-122)

Seeking to ensure that Van Buren would replace Calhoun as his running mate, Jackson had arranged for a national convention of his supporters.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198410%E2%80%9311-123) The May[1832 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1832_Democratic_National_Convention "1832 Democratic National Convention") subsequently nominated Van Buren to serve as the party's vice presidential nominee.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilbey200281%E2%80%9382-124) Van Buren won the nomination over [Philip P. Barbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_P._Barbour "Philip P. Barbour") (Calhoun's favored candidate) and [Richard Mentor Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Mentor_Johnson "Richard Mentor Johnson") due to the support of Jackson and the strength of the Albany Regency.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983300%E2%80%93301-125) Upon Van Buren's return from Europe in July 1832, he became involved in the [Bank War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_War "Bank War"), a struggle over the renewal of the charter of the [Second Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bank_of_the_United_States "Second Bank of the United States").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983301%E2%80%93303-126)

Van Buren had long been distrustful of banks, and he viewed the bank as an extension of the Hamiltonian economic program, so he supported Jackson's veto of the bank's re-charter.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983303,_306%E2%80%93307-127) Henry Clay, the presidential nominee of the National Republicans, made the struggle over the bank the key issue of the [presidential election of 1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._presidential_election,_1832 "U.S. presidential election, 1832").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983307%E2%80%93308-128) The Jackson–Van Buren ticket won the 1832 election by a landslide,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-129) and Van Buren took office as the eighth Vice President of the United States on March 4, 1833, at the age of 50.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-130) During the [Nullification Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullification_Crisis "Nullification Crisis"), Van Buren counseled Jackson to pursue a policy of conciliation with South Carolina leaders.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983321%E2%80%93322-131) He played little direct role in the passage of the [Tariff of 1833](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff_of_1833 "Tariff of 1833"), but he quietly hoped that the tariff would help bring an end to the Nullification Crisis, which it did.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983328-132)

As vice president, Van Buren continued to be one of Jackson's primary advisors and confidants, and accompanied Jackson on his tour of the northeastern United States in 1833.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-133) Jackson's struggle with the Second Bank of the United States continued, as the president sought to remove federal funds from the bank.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983330%E2%80%93332-134) Though initially apprehensive of the removal due to congressional support for the bank, Van Buren eventually came to support Jackson's policy.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983330%E2%80%93334-135) He also helped undermine a fledgling alliance between Jackson and [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster"), a senator from Massachusetts who could have potentially threatened Van Buren's project to create two parties separated by policy differences rather than personalities.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENiven1983355%E2%80%93358-136) During Jackson's second term, the president's supporters began to refer to themselves as members of the Democratic Party. Meanwhile, those opposed to Jackson, including Clay's National Republicans, followers of Calhoun and Webster, and many members of the Anti-Masonic Party, coalesced into the [Whig Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198414%E2%80%9315-137)

### Presidential election of 1836

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Presidential election of 1836")]

Main articles: [1836 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1836_United_States_presidential_election "1836 United States presidential election") and [Second Party System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Party_System "Second Party System")

President [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") declined to seek another term in the [1836 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1836_United_States_presidential_election "1836 United States presidential election"), but he remained influential within the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Democratic_Party "History of the United States Democratic Party") as his second term came to an end. Jackson was determined to help elect Van Buren in 1836 so that the latter could continue the Jackson administration's policies. The two men—the charismatic "Old Hickory" and the efficient "Sly Fox"—had entirely different personalities but had become an effective team in eight years in office together.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-138) With Jackson's support, Van Buren won the presidential nomination of the [1835 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1835_Democratic_National_Convention "1835 Democratic National Convention") without opposition.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-JRIrelan-139) Two names were put forward for the vice-presidential nomination: Representative [Richard M. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_M._Johnson "Richard M. Johnson") of Kentucky, and former Senator [William Cabell Rives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cabell_Rives "William Cabell Rives") of Virginia. Southern Democrats, and Van Buren himself, strongly preferred Rives. Jackson, on the other hand, strongly preferred Johnson. Again, Jackson's considerable influence prevailed, and Johnson received the required two-thirds vote after New York Senator [Silas Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silas_Wright "Silas Wright") prevailed upon non-delegate Edward Rucker to cast the 15 votes of the absent Tennessee delegation in Johnson's favor.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-RMJ9th-140)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-JRIrelan-139)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/ElectoralCollege1836.svg/330px-ElectoralCollege1836.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1836.svg)

1836 electoral vote results

Van Buren's competitors in the [election of 1836](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1836_United_States_presidential_election "1836 United States presidential election") were four members of the Whig Party, which remained a loose coalition bound by mutual opposition to Jackson's anti-bank policies. Lacking the party unity or organizational strength to field a single ticket or define a single platform,[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-RMJ9th-140) the Whigs ran several regional candidates in hopes of sending the election to the House of Representatives.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-141) The candidates were [Hugh Lawson White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Lawson_White "Hugh Lawson White"), [Willie P. Mangum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_P._Mangum "Willie P. Mangum"), Daniel Webster, and [William Henry Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Harrison "William Henry Harrison"). Besides endorsing [internal improvements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_improvements "Internal improvements") and a national bank, the Whigs tried to tie Democrats to [abolitionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States") and sectional tension, and attacked Jackson for "acts of aggression and usurpation of power".[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-preselections-142)

Southern voters represented the biggest potential impediment to Van Buren's quest for the presidency, as many were apprehensive at the prospect of a Northern president.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198417%E2%80%9318-143) Van Buren moved to obtain their support by assuring them that he opposed abolitionism and supported maintaining slavery in states where it already existed.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2007508%E2%80%93509-144) To demonstrate consistency regarding his opinions on slavery, Van Buren cast the tie-breaking Senate vote for a bill to subject abolitionist mail to state laws, thus ensuring that its circulation would be prohibited in the South.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-145) Van Buren considered slavery to be immoral but sanctioned by the Constitution.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-146)

Van Buren won the election with 764,198 popular votes, 50.9% of the total, and 170[electoral votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)"). Harrison led the Whigs with 73 electoral votes, White receiving 26, and Webster 14.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-preselections-142) Mangum received South Carolina's 11 electoral votes, which were awarded by the state legislature.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2007487-147) Van Buren's victory resulted from a combination of his political and personal attributes, Jackson's popularity and endorsement, the organizational power of the Democratic Party, and the inability of the Whig Party to muster an effective candidate and campaign.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MVelections-148) Despite their lack of organization, the Whigs came close to their goal of forcing the election into the House of Representatives, with Van Buren winning the decisive state of Pennsylvania by a little over 4,000 voters, indicating the fragility of the voting coalition that Van Buren had inherited from Jackson.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MVelections-148) Virginia's presidential electors voted for Van Buren for president, but voted for [William Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(South_Carolina_senator) "William Smith (South Carolina senator)") for vice president, leaving Johnson one electoral vote short of election.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-149) In accordance with the [Twelfth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution"), the Senate elected Johnson vice president in a contingent vote.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-150)

The election of 1836 marked an important turning point in American political history because it saw the establishment of the [Second Party System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Party_System "Second Party System"). In the early 1830s, the political party structure was still changing rapidly, and factional and personal leaders continued to play a major role in politics. By the end of the campaign of 1836, the new Second Party System was almost complete, as nearly every faction had been absorbed by either the Democrats or the Whigs.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole1984279-151)

## Presidency (1837–1841)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Presidency (1837–1841)")]

Main article: [Presidency of Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren "Presidency of Martin Van Buren")

### Cabinet

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Cabinet")]

Main article: [Presidency of Martin Van Buren §Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Martin_Van_Buren#Cabinet "Presidency of Martin Van Buren")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Martin_Van_Buren_MET_ap93.19.2.jpg/250px-Martin_Van_Buren_MET_ap93.19.2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin_Van_Buren_MET_ap93.19.2.jpg)

Van Buren as painted by [Henry Inman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Inman_(painter) "Henry Inman (painter)") during his presidency, c. 1837–38

Martin Van Buren was sworn in as the eighth President of the United States on March 4, 1837. He retained much of Jackson's cabinet and lower-level appointees, as he hoped that the retention of Jackson's appointees would stop Whig momentum in the South and restore confidence in the Democrats as a party of sectional unity.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENowlan2012320-152) The cabinet holdovers represented the different regions of the country: Secretary of the Treasury [Levi Woodbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_Woodbury "Levi Woodbury") came from New England, Attorney General [Benjamin Franklin Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin_Butler_(lawyer) "Benjamin Franklin Butler (lawyer)") and Secretary of the Navy [Mahlon Dickerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahlon_Dickerson "Mahlon Dickerson") hailed from New York and New Jersey, respectively, Secretary of State [John Forsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Forsyth_(Georgia) "John Forsyth (Georgia)") of Georgia represented the South, and Postmaster General [Amos Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amos_Kendall "Amos Kendall") of Kentucky represented the West.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

For the lone open position of Secretary of War, Van Buren first approached William Cabell Rives, who had sought the vice presidency in 1836. After Rives declined to join the cabinet, Van Buren appointed [Joel Roberts Poinsett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Roberts_Poinsett "Joel Roberts Poinsett"), a South Carolinian who had opposed secession during the [Nullification Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullification_Crisis "Nullification Crisis"). Van Buren's cabinet choices were criticized by Pennsylvanians such as [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"), who argued that their state deserved a cabinet position as well as some Democrats who argued that Van Buren should have used his patronage powers to augment his power. However, Van Buren saw value in avoiding contentious patronage battles, and his decision to retain Jackson's cabinet made it clear that he intended to continue the policies of his predecessor. Additionally, Van Buren had helped select Jackson's cabinet appointees and enjoyed strong working relationships with them.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198437%E2%80%9340-153)

Van Buren held regular formal cabinet meetings and discontinued the informal gatherings of advisors that had attracted so much attention during Jackson's presidency. He solicited advice from department heads, tolerated open and even frank exchanges between cabinet members, perceiving himself as "a mediator, and to some extent an umpire between the conflicting opinions" of his counselors. Such detachment allowed the president to reserve judgment and protect his prerogative for making final decisions. These open discussions gave cabinet members a sense of participation and made them feel part of a functioning entity, rather than isolated executive agents.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTENowlan2012321-154) Van Buren was closely involved in foreign affairs and matters pertaining to the Treasury Department; but the Post Office, War Department, and Navy Department had significant autonomy under their respective cabinet secretaries.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson1984171-155)

### Panic of 1837

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Panic of 1837")]

Main article: [Panic of 1837](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1837 "Panic of 1837")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Jackson_and_Van_Buren%2C_1837.jpg/250px-Jackson_and_Van_Buren%2C_1837.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_and_Van_Buren,_1837.jpg)

_The Modern [Balaam and His Ass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaam#Hebrew\_Bible "Balaam")_, an 1837 caricature placing the blame for the Panic of 1837 and the perilous state of the banking system on outgoing President Andrew Jackson, shown riding a donkey, while President Martin Van Buren comments approvingly

When Van Buren entered office, the nation's economic health had taken a turn for the worse and the prosperity of the early 1830s was over. Two months into his presidency, on May 10, 1837, some important state banks in New York, running out of hard currency reserves, refused to convert paper money into gold or silver, and other financial institutions throughout the nation quickly followed suit. This [financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_crisis "Financial crisis") became known as the [Panic of 1837](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1837 "Panic of 1837").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MBdomestic-156) The Panic was followed by a five-year [depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(economics) "Depression (economics)") in which banks failed and unemployment reached record highs.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-157)

Van Buren blamed the economic collapse on greedy American and foreign business and financial institutions, as well as the over-extension of credit by U.S. banks. Whig leaders in Congress blamed the Democrats, along with Andrew Jackson's economic policies,[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MBdomestic-156) specifically his 1836 [Specie Circular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specie_Circular "Specie Circular"). Cries of "rescind the circular!" went up and former president Jackson sent word to Van Buren asking him not to rescind the order, believing that it had to be given enough time to work. Others, like [Nicholas Biddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Biddle_(banker) "Nicholas Biddle (banker)"), believed that Jackson's [dismantling of the Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_War#Jackson's_dismantling_of_the_BUS "Bank War") was directly responsible for the irresponsible creation of paper money by the state banks which had precipitated this panic.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-Seigenthaler-158) The Panic of 1837 loomed large over the [1838 election cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_elections,_1838 "United States elections, 1838"), as the carryover effects of the economic downturn led to Whig gains in both the U.S. House and Senate. The state elections in 1837 and 1838 were also disastrous for the Democrats,[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-159) and the partial economic recovery in 1838 was offset by a second commercial crisis later that year.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-160)

To address the crisis, the Whigs proposed rechartering the [national bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_central_banking_in_the_United_States "History of central banking in the United States"). The president countered by proposing the establishment of an [independent U.S. treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Treasury "Independent Treasury"), which he contended would take the politics out of the nation's money supply. Under the plan, the government would hold its money in [gold or silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_money_(policy) "Hard money (policy)"), and would be restricted from printing [paper money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknote "Banknote") at will; both measures were designed to prevent inflation.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-161) The plan would permanently separate the government from private banks by storing government funds in government vaults rather than in private banks.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198458%E2%80%9362-162) Van Buren announced his proposal in September 1837,[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MBdomestic-156) but an alliance of conservative Democrats and Whigs prevented it from becoming law until 1840.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-Morrison456-163) As the debate continued, conservative Democrats like Rives defected to the Whig Party, which itself grew more unified in its opposition to Van Buren.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson198461%E2%80%9362-164) The Whigs would abolish the Independent Treasury system in 1841, but it was revived in 1846, and remained in place until the passage of the [Federal Reserve Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act "Federal Reserve Act") in 1913.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson1984210-165) More important for Van Buren's immediate future, the depression would be a major issue in his upcoming re-election campaign.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MBdomestic-156)

### Indian removal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Van_Buren&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Indian removal")]

Federal policy under Jackson had sought to move Indian tribes to lands west of the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") through the [Indian Removal Act of 1830](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act_of_1830 "Indian Removal Act of 1830"), and the federal government negotiated 19 treaties with Indian tribes during Van Buren's presidency.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-MVforcebehind-166) The 1835 [Treaty of New Echota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_New_Echota "Treaty of New Echota") signed by government officials and representatives of the [Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee") tribe had established terms under which the Cherokees ceded their territory in the southeast and agreed to move west to [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"). In 1838, Van Buren directed General [Winfield Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott") to forcibly move all those who had not yet complied with the treaty.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-167)

The Cherokees were herded violently into [internment camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment_camp "Internment camp") where they were kept for the summer of 1838. The actual transportation west was delayed by intense heat and drought, but in the fall, the Cherokee reluctantly agreed to transport themselves west.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-168)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-169) Some 20,000 people were relocated against their will during the Cherokee removal, part of the [Trail of Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trail_of_Tears "Trail of Tears").[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-newnetherland-170)[Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson "Ralph Waldo Emerson"), who would go on to become America's foremost man of letters, wrote Van Buren [a letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson's_letter_to_Martin_Van_Buren "Emerson's letter to Martin Van Buren")[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-171) protesting his treatment of the Cherokee.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-172)

An estimated 4,000 Cherokee died during the Trail of Tears. Entire Indian nations were relocated, with some losing as much as half their populations. Van Buren claimed that America was "perhaps in the beginning unjustifiable aggressors" toward the Indians, but later became the "guardians". He told Congress that a "mixed occupancy of the same territory by the white and red man is incompatible with the safety or happiness of either", and also claimed the Cherokee had not protested their removal.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren#cite_note-173)

Joseph Robinette Biden Jr.[a] (born November 20, 1942) is an American retired politician who served as the 46th president of the United States from 2021 to 2025. A member of the Democratic Party, he represented Delaware in the United States Senate from 1973 to 2009 and also served as the 47th vice president under President Barack Obama from 2009 to 2017.

Born in Scranton, Pennsylvania, Biden graduated from the University of Delaware in 1965 and the Syracuse University College of Law in 1968. He was elected to the New Castle County Council in 1970 and the U.S. Senate in 1972. As a senator, Biden chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee and Foreign Relations Committee. He drafted and led passage of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act and the Violence Against Women Act. Biden oversaw six U.S. Supreme Court confirmation hearings, including contentious hearings for Robert Bork and Clarence Thomas. He opposed the Gulf War in 1991 but voted in favor of the Iraq War Resolution in 2002. Biden ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic presidential nomination in the 1988 and 2008 primaries. In 2008, Obama chose him as his running mate, and he served as a close advisor to Obama while in office. In the 2020 presidential election, Biden chose Kamala Harris as his running mate, and they defeated Republican incumbents Donald Trump and Mike Pence.

As president, Biden signed the American Rescue Plan Act in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and recession. He signed bipartisan bills on infrastructure and manufacturing. Biden proposed the Build Back Better Act, part of which was incorporated into the Inflation Reduction Act passed in 2022. He appointed Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court of the United States. In his foreign policy, the U.S. reentered the Paris Agreement and enacted the New Atlantic Charter. Biden withdrew U.S. troops from Afghanistan in a chaotic exit, after which the Taliban swiftly retook control. He responded to the Russian invasion of Ukraine by imposing sanctions on Russia and authorizing Ukrainian aid. In 2022, Biden supported Finland's and Sweden's bids to join NATO and formally approved their membership. During the Gaza war, he condemned the actions of Hamas, gave Israel strong military and diplomatic support, sent humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip, and backed a temporary ceasefire proposal before his presidency ended.

Concerns about Biden's age and health persisted throughout his presidency. He is the first president to turn 80 years old while in office. Biden initially ran for reelection in 2024, winning the Democratic primaries and becoming the party's presumptive nominee.
